## Introduction

Payment fraud is becoming more prevalent with the current climate of
e-commerce and the development of different payment methods. In July
2023, the Federal Reserve launched the FedNow Service, which allows
banks and credit unions of any size to send instant payments at any time
of day and every day of the year [@frbservices2023fednow]. As real-time
payment adoption increases, fraud detection models must flag suspicious
transactions as they happen. This increases the need for more robust
ways to identify transaction fraud. Random forest is commonly used to
address this problem. Current research focuses on handling the
unbalanced nature of fraudulent transactions. In this paper we test some
of the common random forest models against the original algorithm to
find which model has greater fraud detection performance.

### Literature Review                                                                        

Random Forest (RF) is a widely adopted machine learning method because
of its computational efficiency and versatility [@scornet2026theory;
@salman2024random]. RF trees are not highly correlated so the risk of
overfitting is relatively low [@salman2024random]. RF was initially
created to run classification and regression tests but has expanded into
other domains like survival analysis and quantile regression. The
subsampling structure allows the uncertainty of its predictions to be
quantified [@scornet2026theory]. RF’s main limitation is prediction
speed. It can train quickly but can be slow when needed for real-time
decisions [@salman2024random].

RF has proven effective for credit card fraud detection
[@jebaseeli2020fraud; @borketey2024; @salunke2025fraud]. @borketey2024
compared it with logistic regression, linear discriminant analysis,
k-nearest neighbors, and classification trees on a dataset with 0.17%
fraudulent transactions with RF detecting about 71% of those
transactions. Some studies used RF that did not adjust for class
imbalance and the authors judged RF mainly on overall predictions
[@jebaseeli2020fraud]. RF has limitations like degrading when the scale
of the dataset increases [@xuan2018random]. Fraud changes over time and
data collection is different by region making it difficult to generalize
[@borketey2024].

Using accuracy as a metric is not the best way to measure performance of
this method when fraudulent transactions are rare. A model can have a
very high accuracy score while missing most of the fraudulent
transactions. For this reason, several studies relied on precision,
recall, F1, and area-under-the-curve measures [@galar2012review;
@borketey2024; @wijaya2024comparative; @aburbeian2023credit].

A common way to deal with data imbalance is to pair RF with SMOTE
[@bhagat2015enhanced; @aburbeian2023credit; @zhang2024improved]. This
combination has improved the minority-class detection outside fraud.
@bhagat2015enhanced applied SMOTE after splitting the multi-class
problem with One-vs-All and One-vs-One methods and @zhang2024improved
combined SMOTE with tree pruning and Z-score normalization and reached
98.03% accuracy and 100% recall. The results do support the general
approach of pairing SMOTE with RF; however, this may not directly
transfer over to fraud detection. SMOTE was found to not always be the
most effective option. Random oversampling with XGBoost achieved the
highest F1-score, 92.43% and the authors concluded that random
oversampling, or undersampling with NCR, gave the best results
[@wijaya2024comparative].

Some methods change how the ensemble samples the data. @galar2012review
reviewed 22 ensemble variants across four families, using a single C4.5
decision tree as the base classifier with AUC for evaluation. The most
complex approaches did not always have the best performance.
SMOTEBagging, RUSBoost, and UnderBagging were the most robust. RUSBoost
provided good performance and was the least complex. @gu2022novel
proposed that an improper sampling strategy can negatively impact model
performance, increase complexity, and cause overfitting. The study also
found that DCI-ISSA-RF, which combines DCI oversampling with ISSA
hyperparameter optimization, outperformed undersampling, most
cost-sensitive methods and baseline RF. However, DCI-ISSA-RF ran longer
on large credit card datasets which relates to the speed concern raised
by @salman2024random.

These studies find that RF is an acceptable choice for fraud detection.
They also provide different techniques for handling class imbalance. The
results are difficult to compare because the studies had significant
variations like different datasets and performance metrics. Some of the
studies did not use cross validation [@wijaya2024comparative] while
others used overall accuracy [@salunke2025fraud] for their results
making it unclear how each imbalance technique improves RF itself. This
study attempts to address the previous study variations by using a
baseline RF and only changing the imbalance treatment. Each approach
will be evaluated on fraud-class precision, recall, F1, and AUC-PR.

## Methodology

### Random Forest

A Random Forest combines many decision trees to make predictions
[@scornet2026theory]. Each tree uses a random sample of the training
data and considers a random subset of features at each split. Combining
the trees generally produces more reliable predictions and reduces
overfitting compared with a single decision tree.

Firstly, each tree is trained on a sample pulled from the training data
with replacement, as a result some observations may be used more than
once.

$$D_b \sim \text{Bootstrap}(D), \quad b = 1, \dots, B$$

where $D$ is the training data, $D_b$ is the sample for tree $b$, and
$B$ is the number of trees.

Second, the trees are built and at each split a random subset of
features is drawn. The best split from those features is used.

Third, predictions are combined. For classification, the forest uses the
majority vote across trees. The share of trees voting fraud serves as
the predicted fraud probability.

### Assumptions

Random Forest does not make assumptions about the distribution of the
data. It does assume that observations are independent and drawn from
the same distribution. This dataset tests those assumptions in two ways.
First, the same users appear in both the training and testing data.
Secondly, the random split ignores the time order of the transactions.
We assume that the fraud labels are correct and that the synthetic data
reflect real world fraud patterns.

### Class Imbalance Treatments

Because splits are chosen to reduce overall impurity, a forest trained
on data with low fraud can perform well overall while missing most fraud
cases. We compare four ways to handle this data imbalance
[@galar2012review].

**Baseline.** This trains a random forest without adjusting the data for
the class imbalance.

**SMOTE.** This method creates synthetic data points for the fraudulent
transactions. It uses that data to train the random forest model
[@galar2012review]. In an effort to prevent data leakage, SMOTE is
applied only to the training data. Data points are generated between a
fraud case and one of its nearest fraud neighbors:

$$x_{new} = x_i + \lambda \left(x_{zi} - x_i\right), \quad \lambda \sim U(0, 1)$$

where $x_i$ is a fraud case, $x_{zi}$ is one of its $k$ nearest fraud
neighbors, and $\lambda$ is a random value between 0 and 1
[@chawla2002smote].

**Balanced Random Forest.** This method trains each tree on a balanced
sample. The model undersamples the non-fraudulent transactions to match
the fraudulent transactions. As a result, each tree uses a different
subset of legitimate transactions.

**Class Weighting.** This method gives fraudulent transactions a greater
weight when choosing splits.

### Procedure

The data is split 70/30 into training and testing sets, stratified on
fraud status. All four models use the same settings and only the
imbalance treatment is changed. Fraud is predicted when the fraud
probability exceeds 0.5. The model for each condition is then assessed
once on the testing set.

### Evaluation Metrics

All metrics are calculated for the fraud class. Accuracy is excluded
because a model can be highly accurate but still miss fraudulent
transactions.

$$\text{Precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP}, \qquad
\text{Recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \qquad
F_1 = \frac{2 \cdot \text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

TP is fraud correctly flagged, FP is legitimate transactions wrongly
flagged, and FN is fraud that was missed [@aburbeian2023credit]. AUC-PR
is the area under the precision-recall curve across all thresholds.

## Analysis and Results

### Data Exploration and Visualization

Our dataset contains 10,000 synthetic financial transactions from August
2025 to August 2026 with 2,142 unique users. The data was obtained from
Kaggle [@greatcool2026financial]. Of the 10,000 transactions only 126 or
1.26% of them are fraudulent. There are no missing values or duplicate
transactions. The dataset contains 11 variables including the target
variable “is_fraud”. The 10 other variables are:

Transaction_id: An identification variable that identifies each unique
transaction

Timestamp: A datetime variable that has the time of each transaction

User_id: this is an identification variable for each user

Account_type: this is a categorical variable that lists the type of
account that was used in the transaction such as savings or checking
account

Category: A categorical variable that describes what type of product was
purchased such as electronics or groceries

Amount: A numeric variable that shows the value of the transaction in US
dollars

Currency: A category variable that shows what kind of currency was used
for example USD

Payment_method: A categorical variable that names what was used for the
payment for example debit card or credit card

Device_type: categorical variable the names the type of machine that was
used such as a POS machine or ATM

Risk_score: A numeric variable that is between 0 to 100 that represents
the predicted risk of the transaction with 0 being the lowest risk and
100 being the highest risk.

Is_fraud: The target variable that determines if a transaction was
fraudulent or not with a 1 being fraud and 0 representing a non-fraud
transaction.

```{r, warning=FALSE, echo=T, message=FALSE}
# loading packages 
library(tidyverse)
library(gtsummary)
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(ranger)
library(themis)
library(PRROC)

```

```{r load-data, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Load data
fraud_df <- read_csv("synthetic_financial_transactions.csv") %>%
  mutate(is_fraud = factor(is_fraud, levels = c(0, 1),
                           labels = c("Legitimate", "Fraud")))

# Numeric copy of the target for fraud rate summaries
fraud_data <- fraud_df %>% mutate(fraud_num = as.numeric(is_fraud == "Fraud"))

fraud_summary <- fraud_data %>%
  count(fraud_num, name = "count") %>%
  mutate(percent = count / sum(count) * 100)

ggplot(fraud_summary, aes(x = factor(fraud_num), y = count, fill = factor(fraud_num))) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(count, " (", round(percent, 2), "%)")), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("0" = "Legitimate", "1" = "Fraud")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("0" = "gray60", "1" = "firebrick")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count of Transactions") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

*Figure 1. Class distribution of legitimate and fraudulent transactions*

*Figure 4. Fraud rate by payment method*

Table 1 compares legitimate and fraudulent transactions. Risk score was
the only variable that had a significant difference between the groups
with a p-value \<0.001. Transaction amount, account type, merchant
category, payment method, and device type showed no significant
difference. Model performance will likely depend on the risk score.

The Fraudulent vs Non-Fraudulent Transactions plot shows the data
imbalance, with only 1.26% of the 10,000 transactions marked as
fraudulent. The Fraud Rate by Category and Fraud Rate by Payment Method
plots indicate that Travel had the highest fraud rate at 1.58% and debit
card had the highest by payment method at 1.36%; however, the
differences between the groups are small and were not statistically
significant per Table 1. The small number of fraud cases in each group
makes these rates unreliable.

### Modeling and Results

### Data Processing

This dataset contained 10,000 synthetic transactions with 11 columns and
no missing values. The data had a severe imbalance of 1.26% fraudulent
transactions for the population. Transaction_id and User_id were dropped
from the model to prevent the model from using  them as identifiers for
fraudulent transactions. Timestamp was dropped since time was not used
as an indicator in this experiment. Currency was also dropped since all
transactions are in USD. A total of six predictors were used: four
categorical (account type, category, payment method, and device type)
and two numeric (amount and risk score). SMOTE requires numeric inputs
so the four categorical predictors were converted to 0/1. The four
models were evaluated using 10 repeated stratified splits 70/30 with
SMOTE applied only to the training data.

### Results

Baseline AUC-PR was 0.096, while random guessing resulted in 0.013; the
models performed better than random guessing. The imbalance methods did
not improve the model’s ability to separate legitimate and fraudulent
transactions. Class weighting matched baseline at 0.096, Balanced RF
scored 0.084 performing very similar to baseline, and SMOTE was the
least effective at 0.055.
```{r}
#| include: false
library(ranger)
library(themis)
library(PRROC)

model_data <- fraud_df %>%
  select(-transaction_id, -user_id, -timestamp, -currency) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

y <- factor(model_data$is_fraud, levels = c("Legitimate", "Fraud"),
            labels = c("legit", "fraud"))

X <- as.data.frame(model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = select(model_data, -is_fraud)))
names(X) <- make.names(names(X))

stratified_split <- function(y, p = 0.7) {
  idx <- unlist(lapply(levels(y), function(l) {
    i <- which(y == l)
    sample(i, floor(p * length(i)))
  }))
  sort(idx)
}

evaluate <- function(prob_fraud, truth, threshold = 0.5) {
  pred <- ifelse(prob_fraud >= threshold, "fraud", "legit")
  tp <- sum(pred == "fraud" & truth == "fraud")
  fp <- sum(pred == "fraud" & truth == "legit")
  fn <- sum(pred == "legit" & truth == "fraud")
  precision <- if ((tp + fp) == 0) NA else tp / (tp + fp)
  recall <- tp / (tp + fn)
  f1 <- if (is.na(precision) || (precision + recall) == 0) 0 else
    2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
  auc_pr <- pr.curve(scores.class0 = prob_fraud[truth == "fraud"],
                     scores.class1 = prob_fraud[truth == "legit"])$auc.integral
  c(precision = precision, recall = recall, f1 = f1, auc_pr = auc_pr)
}

n_trees <- 500
methods <- c("Baseline RF", "SMOTE", "Balanced RF", "Class weights")

fit_predict <- function(method, X_tr, y_tr, X_te) {
  train <- data.frame(X_tr, Class = y_tr)
  if (method == "SMOTE") {
    train <- smote(train, var = "Class", k = 5, over_ratio = 1)
  }
  n_f <- sum(train$Class == "fraud"); n_l <- sum(train$Class == "legit")
  args <- list(Class ~ ., data = train, num.trees = n_trees,
               probability = TRUE, seed = 1)
  if (method == "Balanced RF") {
    frac <- n_f / nrow(train)
    args$sample.fraction <- c(frac, frac)
    args$replace <- TRUE
  }
  if (method == "Class weights") {
    args$class.weights <- c(1, n_l / n_f)
  }
  fit <- do.call(ranger, args)
  predict(fit, data = X_te)$predictions[, "fraud"]
}
##| include: false
seeds <- 1:10
results <- list()
risk_results <- numeric(length(seeds))

for (s in seeds) {
  set.seed(s)
  tr <- stratified_split(y)
  for (m in methods) {
    p <- fit_predict(m, X[tr, ], y[tr], X[-tr, ])
    results[[length(results) + 1]] <-
      c(seed = s, method = m, as.list(evaluate(p, y[-tr])))
  }
  rs <- model_data$risk_score[-tr]
  truth <- y[-tr]
  risk_results[s] <- pr.curve(scores.class0 = rs[truth == "fraud"],
                              scores.class1 = rs[truth == "legit"])$auc.integral
}

res <- bind_rows(lapply(results, as.data.frame))
res[, c("precision", "recall", "f1", "auc_pr")] <-
  lapply(res[, c("precision", "recall", "f1", "auc_pr")], as.numeric)

base_auc <- res %>% filter(method == "Baseline RF") %>% arrange(as.numeric(seed)) %>% pull(auc_pr)
risk_wins <- sum(risk_results > base_auc)
```


```{r tbl-results}
#| tbl-cap: "Model performance on the fraud class across 10 stratified splits, mean (SD). Precision is undefined when a model predicted no fraud cases. Threshold metrics use a 0.5 cutoff."
fmt <- function(m, s) ifelse(is.na(m), "Undefined", sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", m, s))

model_rows <- res %>%
  group_by(method) %>%
  summarise(across(c(auc_pr, recall, precision, f1),
                   list(m = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), s = ~sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))) %>%
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = methods)) %>%
  arrange(method) %>%
  transmute(Model = as.character(method),
            `AUC-PR` = fmt(auc_pr_m, auc_pr_s),
            Recall = fmt(recall_m, recall_s),
            Precision = fmt(precision_m, precision_s),
            F1 = fmt(f1_m, f1_s))

reference_rows <- tibble(
  Model = c("Random guessing", "Risk score only"),
  `AUC-PR` = c(sprintf("%.3f", mean(y == "fraud")),
               sprintf("%.3f (%.3f)", mean(risk_results), sd(risk_results))),
  Recall = "", Precision = "", F1 = ""
)

knitr::kable(bind_rows(reference_rows, model_rows), align = "lcccc")
```

The data limited the models’ ability because risk score was the main
variable that identified the difference between legitimate and
fraudulent transactions. Risk score alone reached an AUC-PR of 0.116
compared with 0.096 for baseline RF. It scored higher on 8 out of 10
splits. While the Random Forest used other variables to help identify
fraudulent transactions, it is likely those variables added noise to the
model.

```{r fig-distribution}
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of each metric across 10 stratified splits by model."
res %>%
  pivot_longer(c(auc_pr, recall, precision, f1), names_to = "metric") %>%
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = methods),
         metric = recode(metric, auc_pr = "AUC-PR", recall = "Recall",
                         precision = "Precision", f1 = "F1")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(method, value)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))
```

Baseline RF assigned every transaction a low probability of fraud
because there was only 1.26% of fraudulent cases resulting in recall of
0. The model requires the transactions to have a 50% probability before
identifying them as fraudulent. Class weighting and baseline precision
remain undefined due to their inability to identify fraudulent
transactions. Balanced RF identified about 31% of the fraudulent
transactions with precision being 3%. However, its ranking did not
improve with an AUC-PR of 0.084 which is similar to the baseline score
of 0.096.  The models were limited due to the fraudulent transactions
being very similar to legitimate transactions.

```{r fig-AUC-PR}
#| fig-cap: "Precision-recall curves for one stratified split (seed 1). The dashed line is the fraud rate, the expected precision of random guessing."
set.seed(1)
tr <- stratified_split(y)
pr_df <- bind_rows(lapply(methods, function(m) {
  p <- fit_predict(m, X[tr, ], y[tr], X[-tr, ])
  pr <- pr.curve(scores.class0 = p[y[-tr] == "fraud"],
                 scores.class1 = p[y[-tr] == "legit"], curve = TRUE)
  data.frame(recall = pr$curve[, 1], precision = pr$curve[, 2], method = m)
}))

ggplot(pr_df, aes(recall, precision, color = method)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(y == "fraud"), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Recall", y = "Precision", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```
